new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is confined to the last two syllables and is weight-driven: a word-final superheavy syllable (CVVC, CVCC) takes the stress; otherwise the penult is stressed as a heavy syllable (CVV/CVC), and if the penult is an open light syllable its vowel is lengthened so that it can carry stress. Metrically: final-consonant extrametricality, a single non-iterative moraic trochee built from the right edge, End Rule Right, no degenerate feet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 76: 'There does not appear to be any secondary stress in MP, and light syllables never receive any stress.' Only one foot is built per monomorphemic word.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress never extends further left than the penult; a stressed open penult lengthens its short vowel (/so.ti/ -> [ˈsoː.ti]); light CV syllables are never stressed; four-syllable compounds (e.g. [zə.mi.ˈdar.ni]) follow the same right-edge weight rule; English loanwords show speaker-group variation between the MP rule and retained English stress (chs 6-8). Tone from Punjabi borrowings is marginal and does not contradict a stress analysis (p. 26).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress in native (non-loan) Mirpur Pahari vocabulary, monomorphemic words up to three syllables and some compounds; based on native-speaker intuitions and elicited citation forms (author is a native speaker), formalised in Hayes-style metrical parameters and OT. Superheavy syllables occur only word-finally.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Mirpur Pahari (the Mirpuri dialect of Pahari-Pothwari spoken in Mirpur district, Azad Kashmir, and by the UK diaspora; listed as a dialect under paha1251 in Glottolog, dialect glottocode not verified here). Khan's work (2011-2021) describes the Poonch dialect (Rawalakot, Azad Kashmir); Kogan 2011 describes Pothohari of the Rawalpindi plateau and says stress there is unstudied while three tones contrast. Khan & Bukhari 2015 (not opened) reportedly call Poonch Pahari 'unbounded' with superheavy syllables stressed anywhere, so a dialect difference in the stress window is possible and should be checked before generalising to the whole language.

sources.note: Mirpur Pahari has a quantity-sensitive stress system: stress on a final superheavy syllable (CVVC/CVCC); otherwise on a heavy penult (CVV/CVC), with short vowels in an open stressed penult lengthened; stress never further left than the penult; no secondary stress; light syllables never stressed. Author states it is the first description of MP syllable phonotactics and stress.
